entry.title: An Empire of People
entry.content:
Empire of AI opens on Friday, November 17, 2023, around noon Pacific time, when Sam Altman logs on to a video call and four of his five board members tell him he is fired. The prologue runs through all five days: the all-hands where Ilya Sutskever cannot explain anything, the threats from the executives, the employee letter, Microsoft’s offer, Sutskever’s change of heart, Altman’s return. Then the book goes back to a dinner at the Rosewood hotel in 2015, and only in its last part, from inside the board’s deliberations, does it reach the same five days again.

Karen Hao had followed OpenAI since 2019, when she spent three days embedded in its office and wrote the first profile of the company. The book rests on some 300 interviews with around 260 people, more than 90 of them current or former OpenAI staff, and on memos, emails, and Slack messages. Altman and OpenAI chose not to cooperate. It shows in both directions: she knows who said what in which meeting, and Altman is mostly seen through the people who worked with him.

I give it 7.5 out of 10. It is the book to read if you want to understand Sam Altman, OpenAI, and the feuds that shaped both, and it convinced me of something I had suspected: a company that may matter as much as any company in history is still run by people like you and me, a little smarter, a little more cunning, and a little more visionary.

Two books, one story

I read it right after Sebastian Mallaby’s biography of Demis Hassabis, The Infinity Machine, and that turned out to be the right order. Mallaby tells the genesis of DeepMind and, along the way, the genesis of modern machine learning, in chronological order, up to the transformer-based language models whose consequences we are only beginning to live through. Hao tells the other half: the same years, many of the same people (Musk, Sutskever, Amodei, Hinton, Suleyman), seen from San Francisco instead of from London. The two books mirror each other’s blind spots. Mallaby had Hassabis’s cooperation and drew Altman through his rivals; Hao had no cooperation from Altman and draws Hassabis, when he appears at all, from a distance.

Some scenes appear in both and are better for it. Musk’s fear of Hassabis, which Mallaby reports from London, is in Hao’s first chapter as the reason OpenAI exists at all: Musk wanted the future of AI not to be controlled by Larry Page, and Altman emailed him that it would be good for someone other than Google to build it first. A former DeepMind researcher tells Hao that OpenAI’s founding was “a semi-hysterical reaction to a fairly mild-mannered man.” And where Mallaby shows DeepMind dismissing language as the road to intelligence, Hao shows the memo that changed its mind: Geoffrey Irving, a safety researcher who left OpenAI for DeepMind in 2019, brought with him the case for scaling language models (chapter 7). I drew the people and ideas that both books cover, with a source for every link, in Who contributed to AI.

The difference in emphasis is large. Mallaby explains the technology, twice for every idea, and the people serve the history of the field. Hao is interested in the people and the politics, and in who pays for the technology rather than how it works. Both are legitimate choices. Hers makes the better thriller and the weaker history of ideas.

How it is told

Hao writes for suspense, and I appreciated it. These stories are so intertwined, and so interesting on a human level, that they deserve to be told as a drama: the Rosewood dinner, Musk’s ultimatum and exit in 2018, Bill Gates being won over by a demo of GPT-2 and then by GPT-4 passing his biology exam, the Amodei siblings leaving with a third of the GPT-3 team to found Anthropic, and ChatGPT itself. It was rushed out in November 2022 on a rumour that Anthropic was about to ship a chatbot, framed internally as a “low-key research preview”, and staff placed bets on whether a few thousand or tens of thousands of people would try it over the weekend. It had a million users in five days.

The structure is less kind to the reader. The book is in four parts and broadly in order, but it tells several stretches twice. Chapters 2 and 3 tell the years from 2015 to 2019 as the story of an institution, and chapter 5 goes back and tells them again as the story of the research. Chapter 4 leaves OpenAI entirely for an essay on the history of AI from the cotton gin to Dartmouth to deep learning. Chapter 9 moves between Kenya in 2021, Venezuela’s collapse, Colombia, and Nairobi in 2023. Chapter 13 takes up 2023 again from the side of Washington. After Mallaby’s strictly chronological account I sometimes lost track of where in the timeline I was. It did not stop me reading, but a timeline or a list of the cast at the back would have helped, and the book has neither.

The bet on language

Some of the best material is in chapter 5, on the decisions that made GPT. Hao reports that Ilya Sutskever’s framing inside OpenAI was “Intelligence is compression”: a model trained to generate convincing text has to compress what it learns about the world into its essence. Dario Amodei then runs research as a portfolio of bets, and the bet he keeps is GPT-2, which stood for what the field called the “pure language” hypothesis: that a system trained on enough text and nothing else could become generally intelligent, against the “grounding” hypothesis that it would also need perception and action. Amodei came to see scaling language models as perhaps the fastest path, though likely not the only thing needed.

Put next to Mallaby, this is the decisive fork of the decade. DeepMind’s business plan of 2010 dismissed the idea that language is intelligence expressed, and Hassabis spent years believing a model had to act in the world to understand it. OpenAI bet the other way, and won the first round. That compression and pure language are two halves of one wager, that text is enough, is my reading, not Hao’s. She calls the arguments some staff made for the language bet, by analogy to Helen Keller and blind people, “repugnant”, and in chapter 4 she argues that scaling is “a self-fulfilling prophecy”, not a natural law. The book shows the fork clearly anyway.

Three other passages from the first half became notes of their own: a Chinese researcher’s view that no one outside Silicon Valley would have funded this before it had a use (A billion without a plan), the Rickover quote Altman had painted on the office walls (One person can make a difference), and the film Her as OpenAI’s picture of what AGI should feel like (The interface that disappears).

How a mission moves

The passage I will remember longest is in chapter 18, “A Formula for Empire”. Hao argues that OpenAI’s mission works as a formula with three ingredients: it gathers talent around a grand ambition, it gathers capital by making the alternative look dangerous, and it is vague enough to be reinterpreted whenever that suits the company. As evidence for the third, she lists what the mission was said to mean at each stage, each time in the company’s own words:

YearWhat the mission was said to meanWhere it was said
2015A nonprofit “unconstrained by a need to generate financial return”, open-sourcing its researchThe launch announcement
2016Everyone should benefit from AI once it is built, but the science need not be sharedSutskever, in an email to Altman, Brockman, and Musk
2018 to 2019A capped-profit structure to raise the resources the work needed, while avoiding a race without time for safetyThe charter
2020The model walled off behind an API, as “a strategy for openness and benefit sharing”Altman, replying to Hao’s first profile of the company
2022“Iterative deployment”, and racing to ship ChatGPTHao’s summary of the company’s line
2024Putting very capable AI tools in people’s hands for free, or at a great priceAltman’s blog, after GPT-4o

The chapter opens with Altman praising a book of Napoleon’s sayings, in particular how Napoleon reinterpreted the motto of the revolution to consolidate his own power. The parallel is pointed, and Hao means it to be. I read the table differently. Every step has a reason that made sense at the time: training runs got expensive, so the nonprofit needed capital; capital needed a return, so the model needed a business; competitors appeared, so the business needed speed. The idealism of 2015 was not abandoned by one decision. It was worn down by the realities of compute, money, and competition, one reasonable step at a time, by people who mostly still believed they were serving it. That is a process larger than any single person in it, Altman included, and I suspect it would have happened under any of the founders.

The same process shows in a smaller story in chapter 11. In a 2020 memo Altman wanted OpenAI to stay “small, focused, high-trust, low-bullshit, and intense”, and in late 2022 he argued for no more than about a hundred new hires while other executives wanted five times that. OpenAI had about 300 people at an off-site in October 2022 and was close to 800 a year later. Every large group ends up spending more of its work on holding itself together, in a ministry as in a corporation, and I wrote down my own version of that observation in Small, focused, high-trust.

Where I part ways

Hao writes from a clear position, and she says so in the author’s note: the book is “not a corporate book” but “a meditation on power”, and she embedded with communities around the world who live with AI’s costs. In the prologue she states the metaphor plainly. The AI companies are empires in the colonial sense: they seize resources that are not their own, exploit the labour of others, and justify it with ideas of modernity and a race against rival empires. That makes for honest reporting, and in places it makes for a book that reads as a case against the people building AI rather than an account of them. Some of the chapters on the costs borne elsewhere felt longer than their point, and could have been condensed.

One of them I would not cut. Chapter 7, “Science in Captivity”, follows Timnit Gebru, an Ethiopia-born researcher who came to the United States as an Eritrean refugee in her teens and co-led Google’s ethical AI team. She had co-authored “Gender Shades” with Joy Buolamwini, which showed that commercial face analysis failed most often on darker-skinned women. When GPT-3 arrived she warned that a model trained on Reddit and the rest of Common Crawl would absorb its toxicity, and with Emily M. Bender she wrote “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots”. Google ordered her to retract the paper. She set conditions and said she would leave if they were not met; on December 2, 2020, Google told her it was accepting her resignation immediately, and she announced that she had been fired. Hao’s larger point is about science: after this, and after ChatGPT, the industry stopped publishing what its models were trained on, and you cannot test a model honestly if you cannot see its training data. I remembered the debate from the early days of GPT, when bias in the weights was what everyone talked about. In my own work that problem has receded since: a model that looks facts up with tools before it answers gets them right far more often than one answering from its weights. That is not the same as having no bias in the weights, but it changed how much it matters. Hao’s point about closed training data stands either way.

The chapter on Chile, “Plundered Earth” (chapter 12), I found hard to read. Hao tells Chile’s story through its colonial past, the Chicago Boys, Pinochet’s privatisations, inequality, and the election of Gabriel Boric, and she places it among the countries of the Global South that supply the empire with copper, lithium, land, and water for data centres around Santiago. I am fond of Chile and know people there, and that is one lens on the country, not the whole of it. Chile ranks highest in Latin America on the UN’s Human Development Index. Its government courts data centres because it wants the investment, and Hao’s own reporting shows a country deciding for itself: a referendum in Cerrillos, an environmental court that in 2024 ruled Google could not build a water-cooled data centre in Santiago, and a ministry that now drafts its data centre strategy with the activists at the table. By global standards Chile is a sensible place for data centres and mines, and water in a long drought is a fair concern. Hao’s sources are more careful than her framing here. The Indigenous activist Sonia Ramos says her ancestors were miners and the problem is the scale; the Uruguayan researcher Daniel Pena says the same of data centres.

Scale is exactly where I part ways. The bet that Altman, Hassabis, and others make is that spending the world’s resources on building more intelligence will repay itself, by solving problems that we cannot solve without it. Energy is the largest of them. Hao reports that Altman liked to say the energy problem of his largest data centres would solve itself with a breakthrough in nuclear fusion, and that Helion, a fusion company, is his largest personal investment. She quotes a researcher who calls the claim that AGI will solve our environmental problems impossible to prove. It is. It may also be wrong. But it is a coherent strategy, and it deserves more sympathy than the book gives it. Empires are not a net negative by definition. Power concentrated in a few hands makes harm possible, and that is worth debating; the question is what is done with the power once it is accumulated, not the accumulation itself. I made a version of this argument about capital in A billion without a plan.

How the empire falls

The epilogue gives Hao’s alternative. Te Hiku Media, a Māori radio station in the far north of New Zealand, built the first speech-recognition model for te reo Māori from 310 hours of recordings that the community donated with consent, trained on two GPUs of its own. Hao sets it against OpenAI’s Whisper, trained on 680,000 hours taken from the web. Then, borrowing from a talk by the Stanford researcher Ria Kalluri, she names three axes of power: knowledge, resources, and influence. In her account the AI companies control knowledge by concentrating talent, eroding open science, and sealing their models from scrutiny; they control resources by gathering funding, data, labour, compute, energy, and land; and they control influence through ideology and demonstrations that capture the world’s imagination. Her remedy for the third is public education, and she ends with Joseph Weizenbaum, the creator of ELIZA, on what happens once a program’s workings are explained plainly enough to be understood: “its magic crumbles away.”

The axes are a useful lens, and I will use them. Te Hiku is a good story, and small models trained on data people chose to give are part of the future. The detail I find most important is easy to miss: Te Hiku bought its own GPUs, so it did not depend on any tech giant’s cloud. Ownership of the hardware is the part of the resources axis that ordinary people can actually change.

Training bespoke models is one way to do that. Running them is the other, and it is where more and more of the compute goes, every time someone asks a model anything. That is the problem I work on with Archipelag.io: a network in which AI jobs run on GPUs operated by people and communities rather than by a handful of hyperscalers, preferring hosts nearby and recording where every job ran. It is in open beta, and it will not train the next frontier model. But it lets people own a piece of the infrastructure that runs AI instead of only renting access to it, with what comes with ownership: income for the people who host, data that stays closer to home, and no single landlord who can change the terms. The web did the same for publishing. Before it, reaching an audience took a printing press or a broadcast licence; after it, anyone with a computer could put up a page, and the web grew out of millions of people doing exactly that, as I wrote in my review of Tim Berners-Lee’s memoir. Distributed citizen compute is the same move for inference.

I agree completely with the remedy: explaining how these systems work is the best thing anyone can do, and it is what this site tries to do. I part ways where the diagnosis treats concentration itself as the problem, and where small models are offered as a replacement for the large ones rather than as their complement.

Who should read it

Anyone interested in Sam Altman, OpenAI, and the people and feuds behind the technology, ideally after The Infinity Machine, which explains the technology Hao mostly takes as given. The detail is extraordinary, and I came away with more trivia worth remembering than from most books this year. I wish it had stayed more focused: with Hao’s access to the people around Altman, a tighter book about the people alone would have been even grander.

What stays with me is a thread Hao pulls as criticism. The book opens with two epigraphs: Weizenbaum on magic that crumbles once it is explained, and a line from Altman’s blog. In chapter 10 she writes that the Doomers and the Boomers preach from the same bible, one of hellfire and one of heaven. In chapter 18 she comes back to that line of Altman’s, from 2013: the most successful founders set out to create “something closer to a religion”, and a company turns out to be the easiest way to do it. And in chapter 17 she quotes him on a podcast saying that “intelligence is just this emergent property of matter”, which she offers as hype. I share that conviction, and I wrote about it in An emergent property of matter. Where Hao sees a religion as a warning sign, I see an honest description of what these companies are becoming. As the value of human labour falls, they will be held together less by the work they pay for and more by what they believe. OpenAI is one of the first, and its mission will keep moving.

entry.title: The Web Was the Training Set
entry.content:
I read This Is for Everyone on the shore in Okinawa in the autumn of 2025 and wrote about it that winter in Looking back on 2025. That piece was about reefs and the open web. This one is about a sentence I read past the first time and cannot get out of my head a year later, after twelve months of building agent platforms for a living. It is the last line of the last chapter: “AI had aced the Imitation Game, and the web provided the data that made it possible.”

Berners-Lee writes it as a coda. I think it is the thesis of the book, and I think he undersells it.

What the book is

Three books share the binding. The first is a memoir: a boy in East Sheen whose parents wrote code for the Ferranti Mark 1 and knew Alan Turing, physics at Oxford, a homebrew computer built from factory-reject transistors and an adding machine fished out of a skip at a timber yard, a first job at Plessey in Poole. The second is the history everyone buys the book for: CERN, the 1989 memo, the NeXT cube, the first server, Mosaic, the World Wide Web Consortium. The third is a manifesto for the next thirty years: data sovereignty, Solid pods, and an AI that works for you rather than for the company that trained it. Stephen Witt, who wrote The Thinking Machine about Nvidia, is the co-author, and the prose is clean. The structure is looser. The book proceeds by association, which suits its subject, and which is also why some reviewers found it shapeless.

Compressed into one argument: the web won because it was universal and free, both qualities are now being eroded from the inside, and the way out is to give people control of their own data so that the next layer, the agents, works for them. I think he would accept that summary.

The epicentre was not where you expect

The book is strongest as geography. The web did not come out of Silicon Valley, and Berners-Lee is careful to say he barely knew the place existed when he graduated. In 1977, he writes, no Silicon Valley recruiter came to Oxford. His computing education came from his parents, from Manchester by way of Ferranti, and from the strange luck of being born in 1955, the year after Turing died, into a house with the Mark 1’s punch tape on the floor.

Switzerland comes before CERN. His first job abroad was in Zug, writing microprocessor code for a wafer saw, and he dates his attachment to the country to a night of Kaffee Fertig in a chalet above the cows: “I think it was then that I first fell in love with Switzerland. I’m still in love with it today.” CERN follows, first as a six-month contract in 1980 and then as a fellowship from 1984, with an apartment in Saint-Genis across the French border and windsurfing on the lake. The web was conceived in that corridor, at the coffee counter where people from twenty countries worked out how to run a machine nobody fully understood. The 1989 memo says so in its first argument: “CERN is a model in miniature of the rest of the world in a few years’ time. CERN meets now some problems which the rest of the world will have to face soon.”

What I had forgotten is how precarious the whole thing was. The question that hung over the project, in his own phrasing, was “Why, exactly, is the European taxpayer financing the oddball passion project of a thirty-six-year-old computer programmer in the Data and Documents division of a Franco-Swiss particle physics laboratory?” The answer, for three years, was that two managers, Mike Sendall and Peggie Rimmer, chose to hide him from the budget. Sendall’s pencilled “vague, but exciting” on the memo is famous. The chapter around it, about Sendall’s illness and the marriage Peggie entered to be able to care for him in a Swiss hospital, is the most human thing in the book, and it is a reminder that infrastructure gets built because particular people protect it for a while.

The British bookend is the 2012 Olympics, where Danny Boyle asked him to type the title phrase on a NeXT in front of 80,000 people as one of the inventions “Britons had shared with the world.” Between Geneva and London there is the one scene I would put in every history of computing: the 1992 NeXT developer conference in Paris, where Berners-Lee set up the web on a folding table to show Steve Jobs, and an aide pulled Jobs away one table early. He calls it a sliding-doors moment. I think he is right, and I think the door that closed was a European one. Two years later the consortium went to MIT, with a foothold at INRIA. The centre of gravity followed the money.

Free, because Gopher was not

The chapter I would make mandatory reading for anyone who writes policy about open standards is the one about Gopher. Until 1994 more people used Gopher than the web. In February 1993 the University of Minnesota announced that it reserved the right to charge licensees. It never collected a cent, by his account, and the announcement alone killed the protocol within months.

Berners-Lee’s reaction is the part that matters. He realised the web was in the same position: written on CERN machines, on a CERN salary, owned by CERN. “For the web to succeed, it had to be free.” Inside the lab there was a faction, he calls them “patriots”, who wanted the opposite: spin the web out as a company “to prove that Europe could compete” with Silicon Valley. He was sympathetic and overruled them. On 30 April 1993 CERN’s directors signed a statement that “CERN relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code, both source and binary and permission is given to anyone to use, duplicate, modify and distribute it.”

I agree with the decision and I want to be exact about what it cost. Europe funded the research, hosted the invention, and gave away the result without keeping an institution that could compound on it. The protocol stayed free; the platforms built on top of it did not, and none of the large ones are European. That pattern, the commons funded here and captured there, is the background to the argument I made in The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It, and reading this chapter again made me more convinced of it, not less. The public-domain release was correct. The absence of any European plan for what came after was the mistake, and it was not his to make.

The web was the training set

Now the sentence. Berners-Lee’s own account of machine learning is short and, for a man who spent two decades on the semantic web, generous. Machine learning, he writes, “has three legs: software, hardware and data,” and “it is the third leg, the data, that is in many cases the missing piece of the puzzle.” He tells the GPT story with the detail I had not registered: the first GPT trained on a corpus of self-published romance and science fiction, and “its output was closer to nonsense than meaningful human prose.” The models became useful only once OpenAI turned to the non-profit archivists at Common Crawl and trained on the web itself. His conclusion, in the chapter on intelligent machines: “Data was the fuel for this breakthrough” and, specifically, free and open web data.

The numbers back him. In the GPT-3 paper, filtered Common Crawl is 410 billion tokens and 60 per cent of the training mix by weight; the rest is more web (WebText2), two book corpora, and Wikipedia, which is also the web. The 2024 PNAS study he cites as the Turing Test being passed found that a GPT-4 model’s choices in behavioural games were statistically indistinguishable from a random person drawn from tens of thousands of human subjects in more than fifty countries. Whatever one thinks of the framing, the mechanism is not in dispute. The models learned to write from what people had published, and people had published it because of the thing this book describes.

What I want to add is why the web worked as a corpus, because the reasons are design decisions in chapters 2 and 3, not accidents. A page is a document with a stable address. Text is marked up, so titles and headings and lists can be told apart. Links are explicit, so relevance can be computed; PageRank is a graph algorithm over anchor tags, and Common Crawl’s filters and deduplication lean on the same structure. The hash sign, the place where in his words networking and hypertext “meet”, is also where a crawler learns which part of an address is a document and which is a position inside it. He describes the five-star ladder for open government data later in the book: on the web, structured, non-proprietary, addressable, linked. The web as a whole climbed that ladder without being asked, and a quarter of a century of people exposing their writing to each other in a structured, addressable form is what a transformer was eventually pointed at. The commons was the dataset before anyone called it one.

Two consequences follow, and the book reaches the first but not the second.

The first is his. The same openness that let the web grow is why the text could be taken without asking. He is blunt that Common Crawl “contains a lot of copyrighted material” and that the models can reproduce it, and he lands on a position I did not expect from the man who refused to patent HTTP: “An AI should only have the right to use your creative work as input if you have explicitly opted in, and should you opt in, you have a right to get paid.” He proposes a Content ID for text and admits the attribution problem is unsolved, with a GPT-4 ode to a dishwasher in the style of Philip Larkin as the test case. Nothing in it is Larkin’s, and all of it is. This site, for what it is worth, publishes a Content-Signal line in its robots.txt and a llms.txt and asks for attribution, which is roughly his opt-in with the terms attached. Whether anyone reads it is a separate question.

The second is mine. If the web was the training set, then what was never put on the web is not in the models. That is the whole of the European data argument in one line. The archives, the press runs, the parliamentary records, the century of paywalled newspaper pages, the scientific proceedings in twenty-four languages, exist in machine-readable form or could, and sit outside the corpus the frontier models were built from. Berners-Lee’s own life makes the point: the data at CERN only became valuable to physics once his system put it where other people could find it, and the same is true of the data Europe is sitting on now. The next increment of model quality is not in a larger crawl of the same web. It is in the material the web never got.

Where I disagree with him is on the mechanism of intelligence. He argues that scale settles the question: feed a model “a high proportion of all the sentences in the whole world” and “it builds a network with the number of nodes comparable to the number of neurons in your brain.” Parameters are not neurons and the comparison is loose; I read it as enthusiasm, not as a claim he would defend at a whiteboard. He also makes the stronger philosophical claim that there is no difference between simulating consciousness and having it. He is entitled to that view, and I would have liked a chapter on it rather than a paragraph.

Engineering lore

The chapters on the first year of the web are the most fun for anyone who ships software, and they are honest about regret in a way founders rarely are. The URL, in his account, was “the most important thing I ever wrote”, a few lines of code that reduced the friction of moving between machines to a click. The rule for the whole design was to reuse what people already knew: SGML for the markup, DNS for the names, Apollo workstation paths for the addressing. The double slash came from Apollo, and he apologises for it. The DNS order came from the United States, and he wishes he had used the British convention, most general part first, so that addresses read uk.co.widgets.www. The read-write browser he built on the NeXT, where every page was editable, lost to read-only browsers because users preferred one tool for reading and another for writing, and the web became “a lot more passive” than he intended. Marc Andreessen added the IMG tag to Mosaic unilaterally while the argument about a more general design was still running, which is exactly what a public-domain standard permits. The whole first browser, editor and all, was 9,555 lines of Objective-C.

There is a sentence in there for people who build platforms: “software designers, like urban planners, make the mistake of demanding that the user acts like the system, rather than the other way around.” The system behind the web is rigidly modernist, he says; the web on top of it was designed to be an anarchic jumble. Most of the platforms I have seen fail did so by letting the first layer leak into the second.

Charlie, and who the agent works for

The last third of the book is about Solid, the protocol for personal data pods that Berners-Lee has been building since the semantic web years, and about Inrupt, the company he co-founded to commercialise it. The argument runs through a 2017 dialogue with an imagined assistant called Charlie. Charlie reads a chef’s cookbooks as a training set to reconstruct a dish, invests in a start-up to give Bob something in common with his mother-in-law, and when asked who it works for answers: “Legally, ethically and algorithmically, I work for you, Bob.” It was written before ChatGPT, and it reads now like a product spec for the agents everyone is building.

As someone who builds the other side of that spec, I think he has the problem right and the solution only half right. The problem is real: the apps on a phone do not share data because they do not trust each other and do not speak the same language, and the agent that gets access to everything is the one that most needs to be trustworthy. That is the point of a context layer, which I have argued is the product and a write path, not a cache. Pods are a reasonable place to put that layer. They say nothing about who runs the model that reads it, where the inference happens, or what the agent is allowed to do with what it reads, and that is where the agent platforms I work on spend most of their effort. A pod makes the data yours. It does not make the agent yours.

The Solid chapters also read like a pitch, which they are, and Publishers Weekly’s complaint that the scheme “sounds fuzzy and dull” in his telling is fair. The ideas are not dull. The telling is, because it is written from inside the company. I would have cut a third of it.

Verdict

I give it 8 out of 10. The history is first-rate and told by the one person who can tell it, with the Swiss and British years given their due and the Gopher chapter alone worth the price. The AI chapters contain the most important idea in the book, that the web is the reason the models exist, and then leave it to the reader to work out what follows. The Solid chapters are a prospectus. The structure wanders, and the forecast is thin next to the history; John Arlidge in The Times called it 400 pages with no driving narrative, which is harsh and not entirely wrong.

Read it if you build anything on the web or on models trained from it, and read it for the history first. You do not need a technical background; the hardest idea in the book is the hash sign, and he explains it in a paragraph. Pair it with Mallaby’s The Infinity Machine, which I am reading now and which picks up the Hassabis thread this book opens at a Google dinner in 2014. And read the last line again when you are done. He provided the data. The question of what we do with the rest of it is still open, and it is a European question more than he lets on.

References

  • Tim Berners-Lee with Stephen Witt, This Is for Everyone (Macmillan, 2025). Quotations are from chapters 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12, 16 and 18 of the UK edition.
  • CERN, statement of 30 April 1993 releasing the web software into the public domain. CERN’s account, Twenty years of a free, open web, includes Robert Cailliau’s recollection of the six months of legal work behind the one-page document.
  • Tom B. Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020), arXiv:2005.14165. Table 2.2 gives the GPT-3 training mix: filtered Common Crawl, 410 billion tokens, 60 per cent by weight.
  • Qiaozhu Mei, Yutong Xie, Walter Yuan and Matthew O. Jackson, A Turing test of whether AI chatbots are behaviorally similar to humans, PNAS 121 (9), 2024. The study the book cites as the Turing Test being passed.
  • Common Crawl: monthly crawls of roughly two billion pages each; the cumulative archive is commonly cited at more than 250 billion pages, well above the figure in the book. See also my Europe data piece for the Epoch AI estimate of the public text stock and the FineWeb yield after filtering.
  • Sebastian Mallaby, The Infinity Machine: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the Quest for Superintelligence (Penguin, 2026).
  • Other reviews: Publishers Weekly; Tara Shears, Physics World; John Arlidge, The Times, September 2025; James Gleick, How the Web Was Lost, New York Review of Books, 11 November 2025.

entry.title: The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It
entry.summary:
The public conversation about who wins in AI is almost entirely a conversation about hardware. Who has the most accelerators, who controls the fabs, whose export-control list bites whose supply chain. That conversation is real, and I have spent enough time on the compute side to take it seriously. It is also, increasingly, the wrong place to look for the binding constraint.

The people running the largest labs have been saying so out loud. At NeurIPS in December 2024, Ilya Sutskever told a packed room that “pre-training as we know it will unquestionably end,” for the blunt reason that “compute is growing through better hardware, better algorithms and larger clusters, but the data is not growing, because we have but one internet.” He called data “the fossil fuel of AI” and said the field had “achieved peak data.” A month later Elon Musk said the cumulative sum of human knowledge usable for training had been “exhausted” the previous year. Strip away the showmanship and the claim underneath is an engineering claim about a substrate running short.

I want to take that claim seriously and follow it to where it leads, which is not where the hardware conversation goes. If the scarce input is high-quality data, then the interesting question is who holds the data that has not already been consumed. The answer, for a large and specific category of it, is Europe. Not because Europe planned it that way, but because Europe wrote and printed and catalogued for five centuries and then, for the most part, never put the result on the open web.
